paras: The lynching of Ed Maxwell took place on November 19, 1881, at Durand, Pepin County, Wisconsin, when a crowd overpowered the officers guarding Edward Maxwell, alias Ed Williams, and hanged him from a tree in the court-house yard. Maxwell had just pleaded not guilty to the murder of the Coleman brothers and been committed for trial. The case drew national notice for a coroner's verdict that he had died by falling down the court-house steps, and for a feud among Minnesota and Wisconsin papers over what had happened.

Maxwell and his brother Lon, who used the name Williams, were wanted in Illinois for horse theft and burglary when Milton and Charles Coleman tried to capture them near Durand in July 1881 and were both shot dead. According to the Pepin County Courier, Sheriff Killian of Grand Island, Nebraska, captured Ed at a farmhouse in Merrick County in November, while Lon escaped. Ed was brought through St. Paul and Menomonie to Durand on Friday, November 18, amid long-running talk of mobbing the brothers.

People from the surrounding counties came into Durand through the morning, and when the examination was moved to the afternoon the court room and yard were crowded with men, women and children. Before Justice W. B. Dyer, Maxwell gave his name as William Edward Maxwell, pleaded not guilty and waived examination. As six officers, among them Sheriff Peterson, Under Sheriff Miletus Knight and Sheriff Killian, led him downstairs toward the jail, someone cried "hang the son of a b—" and a dozen or more men overpowered them.

A noose was slipped over Maxwell's head at the front door, and the rope jerked him, handcuffed and shackled, onto the porch and across the ground to an oak east of the court house, where he was hoisted about thirty feet. An informant of the Eau Claire Free Press said the 300-foot rope had been laid in advance from the portico to the tree, and that Maxwell struck his head on a pillar and was a corpse when raised. Knight wrote that no more than two minutes passed between the first attack and the hanging.

The body was cut down after fifteen to thirty minutes, by differing accounts, and buried in the village potter's field. A coroner's jury returned the verdict that he "Came to his death by falling from the court house steps and breaking his neck." Sheriff Killian said no effort was being made to bring the lynchers to trial, and no arrest appears in the coverage.

A letter signed "Voice of Justice" threatened to burn Durand unless Governor Smith punished the "alleged officers and mob," and the Durand Courier answered that there was "more rope here." In late December fire destroyed the county buildings and about thirty stores in Durand, and the New York Sun reported it was believed to be revenge for the lynching.

The fullest early account was a Pioneer Press reporter's dispatch, carried by the Chicago Tribune under the headline "JUSTICE. The Red-Handed Desperado at Durand Lynched," which described a courtroom confession of self-defense and a crowd of lumbermen. Local voices rejected it: the Durand paper called the reporter a liar who left two hours before the lynching, and Under Sheriff Knight wrote that it was done by "the best citizens" of the county, unmasked and sober.

Editorial judgment was divided. The St. Paul Globe said Maxwell "fully deserved death" and blamed Wisconsin's abolition of capital punishment, while the Chicago Tribune treated Durand as a symptom of the failure of criminal justice. The Manitowoc Pilot scorned lynchers brave enough only to hang a shackled man and later called the state's failure to punish them a "burning disgrace."

Southern papers seized on the inquest: the Memphis Appeal mocked "the most funnacious coroner on record," and the Jackson Clarion noted that Northern papers were "shocked that a white desperado in Wisconsin" had been lynched.

The Pioneer Press and the Globe's specials said Maxwell repeated a self-defense claim in court and was seized there, one saying he was thrown out a window, while Knight and the Courier said he said nothing beyond his plea and was taken at the foot of the stairs.

chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A crowd took Ed Maxwell, a prisoner charged with murder, from officers at the Durand court house and hanged him from a tree in the court-house yard (A4, A27, A38).

A crowd variously put at 'a dozen or more' to 'a hundred' men overpowered six officers and hanged Maxwell, who had just been committed for trial on a charge of murdering the Coleman brothers, as punishment for that killing (A12, A21, A27, A38). The papers report no race-based motive; the one paper to name his race called him 'a white desperado' (A28).

Independent accounts from the Pioneer Press reporter, the Globe's Durand and Menomonie specials, Under Sheriff Knight, the Pepin County Courier and an Eau Claire Free Press informant agree that a crowd seized and hanged him at the court house on November 19 (A4, A5, A8, A27, A31, A38).

accounts.label: Eau Claire Free Press informant
accounts.gist: A prepared 300-foot rope ran from the portico to an oak 150 feet away; he was jerked off his feet, struck his head on a pillar and was a corpse when raised.

accounts.gist: Found he died by falling from the court house steps and breaking his neck.

accounts.label: 'Voice of Justice' letter

framing.detail: Chicago Tribune headlined 'The Red-Handed Desperado at Durand Lynched' under 'JUSTICE.', then editorialized that the mob showed criminal justice 'almost a failure'.
St. Paul Globe's 'The Natural Result' said he 'fully deserved death' and blamed Wisconsin's abolition of hanging; its Durand special said he 'only received his just deserts'.
Manitowoc Pilot mocked lynchers brave enough only to hang a shackled man and called the state's inaction a 'burning disgrace'.
Southern papers ridiculed the inquest ('most funnacious coroner on record') and turned it on Northern critics of Southern lynching.
Wire briefs ran from Sacramento to Vermont and Arizona, several misplacing Durand in Minnesota.
